# Flow as controlled movement

A flow network is a directed graph whose edges have capacities, plus two
distinguished vertices: a source `s` that may create material and a sink `t`
that may absorb it. Every other vertex is a junction that must pass on exactly
what it receives.

Formally, a flow assigns a number `f(u,v)` to each edge with

```text
0 <= f(u,v) <= c(u,v)                         capacity
sum of flow in = sum of flow out, for v != s, t   conservation
```

and its **value** is the net amount leaving `s`. Conservation means that value
can equally well be measured as the amount arriving at `t`.


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=8mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  src/.style={nd,fill=orange!30,very thick},
  snk/.style={nd,fill=green!30,very thick},
  ar/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,thick,gray!75},
  cl/.style={font=\scriptsize,fill=white,inner sep=1.5pt},
  tg/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60}]

  \node[src] (n1) at (0,0)     {$1$};
  \node[nd]  (n2) at (2.7,1.2) {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (n3) at (2.7,-1.2){$3$};
  \node[snk] (n4) at (5.4,0)   {$4$};

  \draw[ar] (n1) -- node[cl] {$3$} (n2);
  \draw[ar] (n1) -- node[cl] {$2$} (n3);
  \draw[ar] (n2) -- node[cl] {$1$} (n3);
  \draw[ar] (n2) -- node[cl] {$2$} (n4);
  \draw[ar] (n3) -- node[cl] {$4$} (n4);

  \node[tg] at (0,-0.72)   {source $s$};
  \node[tg] at (5.4,-0.72) {sink $t$};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=7.3cm] at (6.5,1.9)
    {\textbf{One network, four questions.} This is the sample input of
     problem A, and every figure in this section uses it.\\[4pt]
     Edge labels are \emph{capacities}. A flow puts a number $f(u,v)$ on each
     edge with $0\le f(u,v)\le c(u,v)$, and every vertex except $s$ and $t$
     must send out exactly what it takes in.\\[4pt]
     \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
       What is the largest flow $s\to t$? & problem A\\
       Which edges form the cheapest barrier? & problem C\\
       How large can a matching be? & problem B\\
       Which projects should be taken? & problem D\\
     \end{tabular}\\[4pt]
     The answer to the first is $5$, and it is \emph{not} reachable by
     obvious paths alone --- that is what the rest of this section is about.};

  \node[font=\scriptsize,align=left,anchor=north west,text width=6.2cm] at (-0.75,-2.05)
    {\textbf{Conservation, read at vertex $2$.} Whatever arrives on $1\to2$
     must leave again along $2\to3$ and $2\to4$ together. Only $s$ may create
     flow, and only $t$ may absorb it.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Four questions in this section all reduce to that one object, and all four
problems use graphs of this shape.

# The residual graph

Everything interesting about flow algorithms comes from one idea: a decision
already made must remain reversible. That is what the residual graph encodes.


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=7.5mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  ar/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,thick},
  cl/.style={font=\scriptsize,fill=white,inner sep=1.5pt}]

  % original
  \node[nd] (u1) at (0,0)   {$u$};
  \node[nd] (v1) at (3.8,0) {$v$};
  \draw[ar,gray!75] (u1) -- node[cl,above=1pt] {$f{=}5,\ c{=}7$} (v1);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north] at (1.9,-0.5) {as the problem states it};

  \draw[->,very thick,gray!55] (4.65,0) -- (5.65,0);

  % residual pair
  \node[nd] (u2) at (6.6,0)  {$u$};
  \node[nd] (v2) at (9.8,0)  {$v$};
  \draw[ar,blue!65] (u2) to[bend left=28]
       node[cl,text=blue!55!black] {residual $2$} (v2);
  \draw[ar,orange!80!black] (v2) to[bend left=28]
       node[cl,text=orange!60!black] {residual $5$} (u2);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north] at (8.2,-0.5) {as the algorithm sees it};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=13.3cm] at (-0.5,-1.6)
    {\textcolor{blue!55!black}{\textbf{Forward residual}} $c-f=2$: how much more
     can still be pushed along the edge.\\[2pt]
     \textcolor{orange!60!black}{\textbf{Backward residual}} $f=5$: how much of
     the flow already there may be \emph{taken back}.\\[4pt]
     The backward edge is not a road that exists in the input. It is
     permission to cancel up to $5$ units of an earlier decision when a better
     global routing turns up. Without it, an algorithm would have to get every
     choice right the first time; with it, no choice is ever final.\\[4pt]
     \textbf{The update.} Pushing $x$ along an edge does two things at once:
     subtract $x$ from the forward residual and add $x$ to the backward one.
     Store the index of the reverse edge, not just the endpoint, or the second
     half of that update cannot be done.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Concretely, if an edge of capacity `7` currently carries `5`:

```text
forward residual  c - f = 2      push at most 2 more
backward residual     f = 5      take back at most 5
```

An augmenting path is any `s`-to-`t` path in the residual graph, and it may mix
forward and backward edges freely. Pushing `x` along it subtracts `x` from each
forward residual and adds `x` to each matching backward residual.

In code, each edge is stored together with the **index** of its reverse edge,
so that both halves of that update are one array access apart. Storing only the
reverse endpoint is not enough: parallel edges between the same pair would
become indistinguishable.

# Dinic's algorithm

Repeatedly augmenting along any residual path terminates, but slowly. Dinic
organises the search into phases:

1. BFS from `s` over edges with positive residual, giving `level[v]`.
2. DFS that may only move from `v` to `to` when `level[to] == level[v] + 1`.
3. Keep sending flow in this level graph until no augmenting path remains.
4. Relevel and repeat; stop when the BFS cannot reach `t`.

The level restriction is not a heuristic. It forbids sideways and backward
moves, so the DFS cannot wander, and each phase strictly increases the length
of the shortest `s`-to-`t` path. That bounds the number of phases by `O(V)`.


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=7.6mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  src/.style={nd,fill=orange!30},
  snk/.style={nd,fill=green!30},
  ar/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,gray!70},
  hi/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,very thick},
  dead/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,gray!40,densely dashed},
  cl/.style={font=\scriptsize,fill=white,inner sep=1.3pt},
  lv/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!55},
  hd/.style={font=\small\bfseries,anchor=west}]

  % ================= PHASE 1 =================
  \node[hd] at (-0.75,2.35) {Phase 1};
  \node[lv,anchor=west] at (0.85,2.35) {levels $0,1,1,2$};
  \node[src] (a1) at (0,0)     {$1$};
  \node[nd]  (a2) at (2.2,1.1) {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (a3) at (2.2,-1.1){$3$};
  \node[snk] (a4) at (4.4,0)   {$4$};
  \node[lv] at (0,0.72)    {$0$};
  \node[lv] at (2.2,1.82)  {$1$};
  \node[lv] at (2.2,-1.82) {$1$};
  \node[lv] at (4.4,0.72)  {$2$};
  \draw[hi,orange!80!black] (a1) -- node[cl] {$2/3$} (a2);
  \draw[hi,blue!65]         (a1) -- node[cl] {$2/2$} (a3);
  \draw[dead]               (a2) -- node[cl,text=gray!55] {$0/1$} (a3);
  \draw[hi,orange!80!black] (a2) -- node[cl] {$2/2$} (a4);
  \draw[hi,blue!65]         (a3) -- node[cl] {$2/4$} (a4);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north,align=center,text=gray!60] at (2.2,-2.15)
    {$2\to3$ joins two vertices of the \emph{same} level,\\
     so it is not in the level graph at all};
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north,align=center] at (2.2,-3.05)
    {blocking flow $=\mathbf{4}$};

  % ================= PHASE 2 =================
  \node[hd] at (6.75,2.35) {Phase 2};
  \node[lv,anchor=west] at (8.35,2.35) {levels $0,1,2,3$};
  \node[src] (b1) at (7.5,0)    {$1$};
  \node[nd]  (b2) at (9.7,1.1)  {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (b3) at (9.7,-1.1) {$3$};
  \node[snk] (b4) at (11.9,0)   {$4$};
  \node[lv] at (7.5,0.72)   {$0$};
  \node[lv] at (9.7,1.82)   {$1$};
  \node[lv] at (9.7,-1.82)  {$2$};
  \node[lv] at (11.9,0.72)  {$3$};
  \draw[hi,green!45!black] (b1) -- node[cl] {$1$} (b2);
  \draw[dead]              (b1) -- node[cl,text=gray!55] {$0$} (b3);
  \draw[hi,green!45!black] (b2) -- node[cl] {$1$} (b3);
  \draw[dead]              (b2) -- node[cl,text=gray!55] {$0$} (b4);
  \draw[hi,green!45!black] (b3) -- node[cl] {$2$} (b4);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north,align=center,text=gray!60] at (9.7,-2.15)
    {relevelling put $3$ below $2$, so $2\to3$ is now\\
     usable; the two saturated edges drop out};
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north,align=center] at (9.7,-3.05)
    {blocking flow $=\mathbf{1}$, \ total $=\mathbf{5}$};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=12.9cm] at (-0.8,-3.65)
    {Phase 1 labels show \emph{flow\,/\,capacity}; phase 2 labels show the
     \emph{residual} left on each edge.\\[4pt]
     \textbf{Four is not the answer.} The first phase saturates both obvious
     routes and stops at $4$, because the only edge that could carry more,
     $2\to3$, runs between two vertices of the same level. A fresh BFS then
     puts $3$ one level below $2$, the edge becomes legal, and
     $1\to2\to3\to4$ carries the fifth unit. A third BFS cannot reach $4$ at
     all, and that is the proof that $5$ is maximum.\\[3pt]
     This is the whole reason Dinic relevels instead of running one DFS: each
     phase strictly lengthens the shortest $s\to t$ path, so there are at most
     $O(V)$ phases.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The pointer array `it[v]`, reset once per phase, remembers how many of `v`'s
outgoing edges have already been exhausted, so no edge is examined twice within
a phase.

Two habits matter more than the rest. Rebuild `level` every phase, and reset
`it` at the same time; a stale pointer array silently skips usable edges.

# Minimum cut

A cut is a split of the vertices into `S` containing `s` and `V - S` containing
`t`. Its capacity is the total capacity of the original edges pointing from `S`
into `V - S`. Edges pointing back into `S` contribute nothing.

Any flow is bounded by any cut, since everything reaching `t` must cross. The
max-flow min-cut theorem says the two optima coincide, and the proof is
constructive: after a maximum flow, take `S` to be the set of vertices still
reachable from `s` in the residual graph.


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=8mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  src/.style={nd,fill=orange!30,very thick},
  snk/.style={nd,fill=green!30},
  ar/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,gray!70},
  cut/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,very thick,red!70!black},
  cl/.style={font=\scriptsize,fill=white,inner sep=1.3pt},
  tg/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60}]

  \node[src] (n1) at (0,0)     {$1$};
  \node[nd]  (n2) at (2.7,1.2) {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (n3) at (2.7,-1.2){$3$};
  \node[snk] (n4) at (5.4,0)   {$4$};

  \draw[cut] (n1) -- node[cl,text=red!60!black] {$3/3$} (n2);
  \draw[cut] (n1) -- node[cl,text=red!60!black] {$2/2$} (n3);
  \draw[ar]  (n2) -- node[cl] {$1/1$} (n3);
  \draw[ar]  (n2) -- node[cl] {$2/2$} (n4);
  \draw[ar]  (n3) -- node[cl] {$3/4$} (n4);

  \draw[red!55,dashed,very thick] (1.15,2.3) .. controls (1.5,0.6) and (1.5,-0.6) .. (1.15,-2.3);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,text=red!60!black,anchor=south] at (1.15,2.32) {the cut};
  \node[tg,anchor=east] at (-0.55,0) {$S=\{1\}$};
  \node[tg,anchor=west] at (1.95,-2.35) {$V\setminus S=\{2,3,4\}$};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=7.1cm] at (6.4,1.95)
    {\textbf{Reading the cut off the residual graph.}\\[3pt]
     After the maximum flow, walk from $s$ using only edges with residual
     capacity left. Here both edges out of $1$ are saturated, so the walk stops
     immediately and $S=\{1\}$.\\[4pt]
     The cut is the set of \emph{original} edges from $S$ to $V\setminus S$:\\
     \hspace*{1em}$1\to2$ of capacity $3$\\
     \hspace*{1em}$1\to3$ of capacity $2$\\
     \hspace*{1em}total $\mathbf{5}$ $=$ the maximum flow.\\[4pt]
     Every such edge must be saturated --- otherwise it would still have
     residual capacity and its far end would have been reached, putting it
     inside $S$. That is the whole proof.\\[4pt]
     Note $3\to4$ carries $3$ of $4$ and is \emph{not} saturated. It does not
     matter: both ends lie outside $S$, so it never crosses the cut. Only
     edges leaving $S$ are counted, and edges re-entering $S$ are ignored.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

That set is exactly what problem C asks you to print, and it costs one extra
BFS after the flow is already computed.

# Bipartite matching

A matching is a set of edges sharing no endpoint. For a bipartite graph the
maximum matching is a maximum flow on a graph built in three lines:

```text
s -> every left vertex            capacity 1
left u -> right v for each edge   capacity 1
every right vertex -> t           capacity 1
```


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=7.2mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  src/.style={nd,fill=orange!30},
  snk/.style={nd,fill=green!30},
  ar/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,gray!55},
  mt/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,very thick,green!45!black},
  tg/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60}]

  \node[src] (s)  at (0,0)     {$s$};
  \node[nd]  (l1) at (1.9,1.35){$1$};
  \node[nd]  (l2) at (1.9,0)   {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (l3) at (1.9,-1.35){$3$};
  \node[nd]  (r1) at (4.1,1.35){$1$};
  \node[nd]  (r2) at (4.1,0)   {$2$};
  \node[nd]  (r3) at (4.1,-1.35){$3$};
  \node[snk] (t)  at (6.0,0)   {$t$};

  \draw[mt] (s) -- (l1);  \draw[mt] (s) -- (l2);  \draw[mt] (s) -- (l3);
  \draw[mt] (l1) -- (r1); \draw[ar] (l1) -- (r2);
  \draw[mt] (l2) -- (r2); \draw[mt] (l3) -- (r3);
  \draw[mt] (r1) -- (t);  \draw[mt] (r2) -- (t);  \draw[mt] (r3) -- (t);

  \node[tg] at (1.9,2.0)  {left};
  \node[tg] at (4.1,2.0)  {right};
  \node[tg,anchor=north,align=center] at (3.0,-2.0)
    {every capacity is $1$};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=7.6cm] at (6.9,2.15)
    {\textbf{Problem B's sample, as a flow network.} Add $s$ with an edge to
     every left vertex, $t$ with an edge from every right vertex, and give
     \emph{every} edge capacity $1$.\\[4pt]
     One unit of flow is one matched pair. Capacity $1$ out of $s$ stops a
     left vertex being used twice; capacity $1$ into $t$ does the same on the
     right. So a maximum integral flow \emph{is} a maximum matching, here of
     size $\mathbf{3}$.\\[4pt]
     \textbf{Why the residual edge matters here too.} Suppose vertex $1$ takes
     right-$2$ first. Then vertex $2$ has nowhere to go --- right-$2$ is its
     only option. The augmenting search does not give up: it walks
     \emph{backwards} along the edge $1\to$ right-$2$, sends $1$ to right-$1$
     instead, and frees right-$2$ for vertex $2$. That backward step is
     exactly the residual edge of the previous figure.\\[4pt]
     The classic augmenting-path DFS used for problem B is this same
     algorithm with the gadget left implicit.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Because capacities are integral, some maximum flow is integral too, so each
edge carries `0` or `1` and the saturated middle edges are a matching. The
capacity-`1` edges at `s` and `t` are what forbid reusing a vertex.

For problem B the usual augmenting-path DFS is shorter to write than a full
Dinic, and it is the same algorithm: "try to give this left vertex a partner,
and if that partner is taken, ask its current owner to move". That request to
move is a backward residual edge, spelled out in plain recursion.

# Implementation and tests

**Edge storage.** Keep one array of edges and, for each vertex, a list of
indices into it. Adding `u -> v` with capacity `c` appends two entries: the
forward edge with residual `c`, and its reverse with residual `0`. Edge `i`
and edge `i ^ 1` are then reverses of each other, which makes the update after
pushing `x` a two-line operation.

**Types.** Capacities and the accumulated flow go in `long long` in C++. Total
capacity out of the source can exceed `2^31` long before `n` does.

**Python.** Write the DFS iteratively or raise the recursion limit; a long
chain of unit capacities reaches recursion depth `O(V)`. Read all input at once
with `sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()`.

| Test | What it catches |
|---|---|
| a single edge `s -> t` | the base case, and off-by-one in vertex numbering |
| two disjoint paths | flow accumulating rather than overwriting |
| a bottleneck edge in the middle | using the wrong minimum along a path |
| sink unreachable from the source | an output of `0` rather than a crash |
| the sample of problem A | an augmenting path that needs a residual edge |
| parallel edges between one pair | merging edges that must stay separate |
| for matching, many left vertices on one right vertex | a DFS that never reassigns |
| for matching, `e = 0` | an empty-input path |

Run the local reference suite with:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/45_flows_and_matchings/check.py
```

# Exercises

Use A to get the edge-and-reverse storage right, because everything else in the
section is built on it. Use B to see that the augmenting-path DFS is the same
algorithm with the gadget left implicit, and test it on a case where a left
vertex must give up its partner. Use C to notice that the cut costs one BFS
after the flow and nothing more, and that `S` is defined by residual capacity,
not by which edges look saturated. Use D as the blind synthesis problem: the
rules are implications, profits may be negative, and the whole task is deciding
what a cut should mean before any code is written. Test a single edge, an
unreachable sink, parallel edges, and a matching instance with no edges at all.

- A. Max Flow: Print the maximum flow from vertex `1` to vertex `n`.
- B. Bipartite Matching: Print the size of a maximum matching between the two sides.
- C. Min Cut Reachable Side: Print the flow value and the source side of a minimum cut.
- D. Project Selection: Choose projects under "if a then b" rules to maximize total profit.
